title: Maximum Number of Occurrences of a Substring
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every length from minSize to maxSize versus recognizing only the shortest length ever needs checking.

content.title: Maximum Number of Occurrences of a Substring

blocks.text: Given a string s, return the maximum number of occurrences of any substring under these rules: the number of unique characters in the substring must be at most maxLetters, and the substring's length must be between minSize and maxSize (inclusive).

blocks.caption: Only substrings of length minSize ever need checking, since shorter never hurts frequency

blocks.text: Given a string s and constraints maxLetters, minSize, maxSize, find the highest occurrence count achievable by any substring that has at most maxLetters distinct characters and a length somewhere between minSize and maxSize.

blocks.title: Analogy: Why Check Every Length When Shorter Always Wins?
blocks.text: Like searching for the most frequently repeated phrase in a speech, but noticing that trimming any qualifying long phrase down to its first few words can only make it appear at least as often (since every occurrence of the long phrase is also an occurrence of its shorter prefix), and trimming can only reduce or keep the same the number of distinct letters used. So there's never a reason to check anything longer than the shortest allowed phrase length.

blocks.caption: A longer substring's frequency is always dominated by its minSize-length prefix, so only that length matters

blocks.text: Before checking every length from minSize to maxSize separately, notice that the maxSize upper bound turns out to be a red herring for maximizing occurrence count.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If a substring of length L (L > minSize) qualifies (has at most maxLetters distinct characters), then its length-minSize PREFIX also qualifies, since a prefix can never have MORE distinct characters than the full substring.

Observation 2: Every occurrence of the length-L substring in s is also an occurrence of its length-minSize prefix at that same starting position, so the prefix's occurrence count is always greater than or equal to the full substring's.

Observation 3: This means the best possible answer can always be achieved by some substring of length EXACTLY minSize; checking any longer length can never produce a strictly better answer.

Observation 4: Slide a fixed-size window of length minSize across s, and for each window that satisfies the unique-character limit, count its occurrences in a hash map, tracking the maximum count seen.

Recognizing that maxSize is irrelevant once this "shorter always wins or ties" argument is established turns an apparently multi-length search into a single fixed-size sliding window pass.

This is the fixed-size sliding window pattern for building a frequency map, combined with the key mathematical insight that the length RANGE constraint (minSize to maxSize) collapses to checking only the single shortest length.
For every length between minSize and maxSize, and every possible starting position of that length, check the unique-character limit and update a frequency map.

items: For every allowed length from minSize to maxSize, and every possible starting position of a substring of that length, count its distinct characters.
If the distinct-character count is within maxLetters, increment its frequency in a hash map, tracking the maximum frequency seen.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every length from minSize to maxSize is tried explicitly, since this version does not yet exploit the "shorter always wins" observation.
A fresh distinct-character check is performed for every substring, since this brute force does not share information between overlapping substrings.
The frequency map naturally accumulates counts across every starting position and length tried.

blocks.text: Every possible substring across every allowed length is checked directly, so the correct maximum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * (maxSize - minSize + 1) * maxSize) in the worst case, accounting for every length tried and the cost of building each substring and its character set.
Space: O(n * maxSize) for storing the substrings in the frequency map.

Limitation: checking every length from minSize to maxSize ignores that longer substrings can never achieve a strictly higher occurrence count than their minSize-length prefixes, making all of that extra work unnecessary.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force checks every length from minSize to maxSize, but longer substrings are always dominated in frequency by their minSize-length prefix. So instead, only ever check substrings of length exactly minSize: slide a fixed-size window of that length across s, and whenever a window satisfies the maxLetters limit, record its occurrence in a hash map, tracking the maximum count seen. maxSize never needs to be referenced at all in the final solution.

Slide a fixed-size window of length minSize across s. For each window, count its distinct characters; if that count is within maxLetters, increment its entry in a frequency hash map and update the running maximum.
Slide a fixed-size window of length minSize across s, tracking a frequency map of qualifying substrings.
Dry run for s = "aababcaab", maxLetters = 2, minSize = 3

codes.python:
def max_freq(s, max_letters, min_size, max_size):
    freq = {}                                                                # note: max_size is never actually used below
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(s) - min_size + 1):                                   # only ever check windows of length min_size
        sub = s[i:i + min_size]
        if len(set(sub)) <= max_letters:
            freq[sub] = freq.get(sub, 0) + 1                                # shorter, more frequent substrings always dominate longer ones
            best = max(best, freq[sub])
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_freq("aababcaab", 2, 3, 4))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * minSize), since each of the roughly n windows costs O(minSize) to build its substring and count distinct characters.
Space: O(n * minSize) for the frequency map in the worst case.

Any qualifying substring longer than minSize has a length-minSize prefix that also qualifies (fewer or equal distinct characters) and occurs at least as often (every occurrence of the longer substring is also an occurrence of its prefix at the same position), so the best achievable frequency is always found among length-minSize substrings alone, making maxSize irrelevant to the final answer.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Window has at most maxLetters distinct characters","Increment its frequency in the hash map and update the running maximum"],["Window exceeds maxLetters distinct characters","Skip it entirely; it never contributes to the frequency map"]]}

items: The window is always exactly minSize characters, built freshly at each position (rebuilding is acceptable here since minSize is capped at 26, keeping the per-window cost small).
A Set (or equivalent) is used to count distinct characters within each window before deciding whether it qualifies.
freq accumulates counts across every qualifying window position, and best tracks the running maximum.

blocks.text: The key insight is entirely mathematical: since occurrence count can only decrease (or stay the same) as substring length increases, the length RANGE constraint collapses to checking only the shortest allowed length, making maxSize irrelevant to the algorithm.

items: Checking every length from minSize to maxSize without first recognizing that longer lengths are always dominated by minSize in occurrence count, wasting significant work.
Forgetting to still check the maxLetters (distinct character) constraint even at the reduced length; the length reduction to minSize doesn't remove that constraint.
Assuming maxSize must play some role in the final algorithm, when in fact it becomes entirely irrelevant once the domination argument is established.

items: Explicitly prove (or at least state clearly) why longer substrings can never beat their minSize-length prefix in occurrence count, since this insight is what allows maxSize to be discarded entirely; skipping this justification makes the solution look like an unexplained shortcut.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Maximize occurrence count over a RANGE of allowed lengths" (as opposed to minimizing or matching a range) points toward checking only the shortest allowed length, since occurrence count is monotonically non-increasing as length grows.

items: How would the approach change if the goal were to MINIMIZE occurrence count instead? Then longer lengths could matter, and every length from minSize to maxSize would genuinely need checking, since occurrence count only decreases (never increases) with length.

How would you optimize the per-window distinct-character count further? A fixed-size array of 26 counters, updated incrementally as the window slides (rather than rebuilt from scratch), can reduce the per-window cost from O(minSize) to O(1) amortized.

What if characters came from a much larger alphabet? The same technique still applies, but the fixed-size counting array would need to become a hash map instead, changing the space complexity slightly.

A fixed-size sliding window combined with a frequency-counting hash map, similar in shape to Maximum Average Subarray I, but the truly decisive step here is a length-reduction argument that eliminates the need to consider a whole range of window sizes at all.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * (maxSize - minSize + 1) * maxSize) time, O(n * maxSize) space.
Optimized (fixed-size window of length minSize): O(n * minSize) time, O(n * minSize) space.

items: Pattern: Fixed-size sliding window (length minSize) with a frequency-counting hash map
Core Idea: Occurrence count can only decrease as substring length grows, so only the shortest allowed length (minSize) ever needs checking
Time: O(n * minSize)
Space: O(n * minSize)
Most Important Observation: A longer qualifying substring's occurrence count is always dominated by its minSize-length prefix, making maxSize irrelevant to the final answer
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Only check length-minSize windows; maxSize is a red herring for maximizing frequency
